a: To our brothers, the Jews in Egypt
t: A book that opens with two letters
p: Before the story begins, the book copies two letters from Judea to the Jews of Egypt, both about keeping Hanukkah.
b:
2 Maccabees opens with two letters (1:1–9 and 1:10–2:18). Only at 2:19 does the writer's own preface begin. Both letters are addressed by Jews in Judea to "the Jews in Egypt," the largest Jewish community outside the land, centered on Alexandria. Both urge them to keep the feast of the temple's purification, Hanukkah.

Since Elias Bickerman's study (1933), most scholars read 1:1–10a as one letter and 1:10b–2:18 as another. Who attached them to the book, and when, is debated: the writer of the book, the writer of the second letter, or the authorities in Jerusalem. See the chapter page.

a: May you have good peace
p: The letter joins the Greek "greetings" with the Hebrew wish for peace, as Jewish letters in Aramaic did.
b: A Greek letter normally opened "X to Y, greetings" (chairein). This one adds "good peace," the Hebrew shalom in Greek dress. Aramaic letters from the Persian period open with a wish for peace in the same place, as in the report to Darius in Ezra: "To Darius the king: all peace" (Ezra 5:7). Bickerman showed that the opening of 1:1 follows the pattern of such Aramaic letters, which suggests the letter was first written in Hebrew or Aramaic, or by someone used to that form.

a: may he remember his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
p: The prayer echoes Exodus, where God "remembered his covenant" before he rescued Israel from Egypt.
b: The words come from the opening of the exodus story: "God remembered his covenant, the one with Abraham, with Isaac and with Jacob" (Exodus 2:24), and from the promise of Leviticus 26:42. Sent to Jews living in Egypt, the wish has an edge: the God who once remembered his people in Egypt will do so again. 1 Maccabees 4:10 has Judas pray the same before a battle.

a: with a great heart and a willing soul
t: A whole heart and a willing soul
p: The wish recalls David's charge to Solomon to serve God "with a whole heart and a willing being."
b: David tells Solomon, "Serve him with a whole heart and a willing being" (1 Chronicles 28:9). The letter's Greek, kardia megalē kai psychē boulomenē, is close to the Septuagint of that verse. The prayer asks for more than outward keeping of the law: it asks God to give the heart that keeps it, as Deuteronomy 30:6 promises.
orig: καρδίᾳ μεγάλῃ καὶ ψυχῇ βουλομένῃ (kardia megalē kai psychē boulomenē)

a: be reconciled with you
p: The Greek katallassō, "reconcile," here speaks of God being reconciled to his people. Paul uses the same verb the other way round.
b: The word family of katallagē, "reconciliation" (here the verb katallageiē, "may he be reconciled"), returns in 2 Maccabees at its turning points: God's anger at his people will end and he will be reconciled to them (5:20; 7:33; 8:29). Paul uses the same word family, but makes God the one who reconciles: "God… reconciled us to himself through Christ" (2 Corinthians 5:18–20; Romans 5:10). Many readers find in the difference a summary of what is new in the New Testament's teaching.

a: in the year 169
p: The year 169 of the Seleucid era is 143/142 BC, under Demetrius II. It dates an earlier letter the writers had sent.
b:
Seleucid dates count from 312/311 BC (see 1 Maccabees 1:10). The year 169 fell in the first reign of Demetrius II (145–138 BC), when Jonathan or Simon led Judea. Most scholars think "we wrote to you" refers to an earlier letter, sent in 143/142 BC, which this letter recalls. The present letter is dated in 1:10a: the year 188, 124 BC.

On that reading, Judeans wrote twice in twenty years to press Hanukkah on the Jews of Egypt. Some take 169 as the date of the present letter itself.

a: after Jason and his people broke away from the holy land and the kingdom
p: Jason bought the high priesthood (4:7–10) and later attacked Jerusalem (5:5–10). The letter dates the troubles from him.
b: The letter writers of 143 BC trace the crisis not to Antiochus IV but to a Jewish high priest. Jason, brother of Onias III, bought the high priesthood and brought in Greek ways (4:7–17). When he lost the office, he attacked the city (5:5–10). "The kingdom" may be the Seleucid kingdom or God's own reign over Israel. Venetus reads that Jason "was sent away" (apestalē) rather than "broke away" (apestē); the KJV has "revolted."
orig: ἀπέστη Ἰάσων καὶ οἱ μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς ἁγίας γῆς καὶ τῆς βασιλείας (apestē Iasōn…)

a: They burned the gateway and shed innocent blood
t: The gate burned, the blood shed
p: 1 Maccabees 4:38 finds the temple's gates burned, and 2 Maccabees 8:33 names a man who set fire to them.
b: When Judas reached the temple, he found "the gates burned down" (1 Maccabees 4:38). 2 Maccabees 8:33 says that Callisthenes and others "set fire to the holy gateways." The phrase "innocent blood" echoes the prophets' charge against Manasseh's Jerusalem (2 Kings 24:4; Psalm 106:38), and here may point to the killings of 5:11–14.

a: and we set out the loaves
p: The letter tells the rededication in four acts: sacrifice, grain offering, lamps and the bread of the Presence.
b: Each act restores a piece of the temple's daily service. The bread laid out before God was to be "in front of me always" (Exodus 25:30). 1 Maccabees 4:50–53 tells the same rededication at length: the lamps lit, the loaves set on the table, the sacrifice offered at dawn on 25 Kislev.

a: the days of the Feast of Booths in the month of Kislev
p: The letter calls Hanukkah "Booths in Kislev." 10:6 explains: it was kept like the Booths the fighters had missed.
b:
Booths (Sukkot) falls in the autumn month of Tishri, and Kislev is three months later. 2 Maccabees 10:6–7 says that the purification was kept for eight days "as one keeps the Feast of Booths," with branches and palms, because at Booths the fighters had been living like animals in the mountains. The name in this letter fits that account.

Booths too lasted eight days, counting its closing gathering (Leviticus 23:36). John 10:22 sets a dispute in the temple at "The Feast of Dedication."

a: In the year 188, at Jerusalem. Those in Judea
p: Swete's punctuation ends the first letter with this date. Venetus, the Vulgate and the KJV begin the second letter with it.
b:
Old manuscripts have little punctuation, so editors must decide where a letter ends. Swete's punctuation puts the date (88 in his text; 188 in Venetus, which the Plain follows) at the close of the first letter, and most scholars since Bickerman agree: the first letter was sent in 188 SE, 124 BC. Rahlfs also ends 1:9 with the date, though he begins the second letter "Those in Jerusalem and those in Judea." The Plain's heading before 1:10 cannot split the verse: its first sentence belongs to the first letter. Venetus puts a stop after "188" and reads "those in Jerusalem and those in Judea," so the date heads the second letter. So do the Vulgate (Anno centesimo octogesimo octavo, populus qui est Jerosolymis) and the KJV.

The second letter would then be dated 124 BC too, though it claims to come from Judas, who died in 160 BC. The variants below give the readings.
orig: ἔτους ὀγδοηκοστοῦ καὶ ὀγδόου ἐν Ἰεροσολύμοις. Καὶ οἱ ἐν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ

a: Aristobulus, the teacher of King Ptolemy
p: A Jewish writer of Alexandria who explained the law of Moses in Greek terms for King Ptolemy VI.
b: Aristobulus is known from fragments quoted by Clement of Alexandria and Eusebius: he wrote for King Ptolemy VI Philometor (180–145 BC), arguing that Greek philosophers had learned from Moses. Clement, about AD 200, mentions him and refers to "the composer of the epitome of the Maccabees," which shows that he read the letters and the book together (Stromata 5.14.97.7). Calling him "teacher" of the king fits the role of a court philosopher, but nothing outside this letter confirms it.

a: the family of the anointed priests
p: The Greek christōn hiereōn, "anointed priests," means priests of Aaron's line.
b: The law calls the high priest "the anointed priest" (Leviticus 4:3, 5, 16), and Aaron's sons were anointed too (Exodus 28:41). The Greek christos here has its old meaning "anointed," not yet the title of the Messiah. The letter honors Aristobulus as a priest as well as a philosopher.

a: the council of elders
p: The gerousia was the governing council of Jerusalem under the Greek kings.
b: The Greek gerousia, "council of elders," appears in a letter of Antiochus III, about 200 BC, which Josephus quotes: the king exempted "the senate," the priests, the temple scribes and the singers from taxes (Antiquities 12.138–142). It later sends envoys to the king (4:44) and receives a royal letter (11:27). The letter sets it between "those in Judea" and Judas, as a body with its own authority.

a: as men who stood in battle against a king
t: Against a king, or with a king?
p: The Greek can mean "as men who fought a king" or "as if God himself had fought the king for us."
b: The phrase hōs an pros basilea paratassomenoi is compressed: "as if lined up against a king." The Plain reads it of the Judeans, who give thanks because their danger was a war with a king. Others read it of God ("we thank him greatly for having fought the king"), which fits 1:12, "he himself flung" the enemy out. The Vulgate has utpote qui adversus talem regem dimicavimus, "since we fought against such a king."
orig: ὡς ἂν πρὸς βασιλέα παρατασσόμενοι (hōs an pros basilea paratassomenoi)

a: flung
p: The verb ekbrazō is used of the sea throwing things up on the shore.
b: The Greek exebrasen is a strong, almost crude word: the sea casts up wreckage and foam. God has "spewed out" the army that fought in the holy city, all the way to Persia. The KJV's "cast them out" is milder. The image prepares for the next verses, where the king meets his death far from Jerusalem.

a: When the leader got there
p: This letter has him killed by priests in a temple. 1 Maccabees 6 and 2 Maccabees 9 have him die of sickness. Historians favor the sickness.
b:
There are three Jewish accounts of the death of Antiochus IV. Here, he is stoned and cut to pieces by the priests of Nanea while trying to take her treasure. In 1 Maccabees 6:1–16 he fails to take the temple at Elymais, falls ill from grief and dies in Persia. In 2 Maccabees 9 he is struck with a pain in his bowels, falls from his chariot, rots alive and, before he dies, vows to set the Jews free and become a Jew himself.

The Greek historian Polybius says he tried to rob a temple of Artemis in Elymais, was driven off, and died at Tabae in Persia, out of his mind (Histories 31.9). Josephus follows 1 Maccabees and argues with Polybius (Antiquities 12.354–359). Many think this letter mixes in the death of Antiochus III, who was killed in 187 BC while plundering a temple in Elymais. See the chapter page.

a: the temple of Nanea
p: Nanea was an old goddess of Mesopotamia and Elam, whom Greeks matched with Artemis or Aphrodite.
b: Nanea (Nanaya) was worshiped in Babylonia, Elam and Persia for two thousand years. Greek writers matched her with their own goddesses: Polybius calls the temple Antiochus tried to rob a temple of Artemis, and Appian a temple of Aphrodite of Elymais (Syrian Wars 66). Temples like hers held great treasure, which made them a target for kings who owed money.

a: as if he would marry her
p: Antiochus claims the goddess as his bride so that her treasure becomes his dowry.
b: In the ancient Near East a king might take part in a "sacred marriage" with a goddess, and Hellenistic kings liked to present themselves as close to the gods; Antiochus IV took the title Epiphanes, "God made manifest" (see 2:20). The trick the letter describes uses religion as a cover for robbery. The letter shows no interest in the rite itself: for its writers the point is that the king who robbed the temple in Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 1:21–24) dies robbing another. A Roman historian, Granius Licinianus, tells a similar story of Antiochus at Hierapolis in Syria: he pretended to marry the goddess there, called Diana, and took her treasures as a dowry (book 28). The place differs, but the trick is the same.

a: the Friends
p: "Friends" (philoi) was a rank at the Seleucid court.
b: As in 1 Maccabees, the court title is capitalized: the king's Friends were his inner circle of nobles and officers (1 Maccabees 2:18; 10:65). In 2 Maccabees the rank returns often (7:24; 8:9; 10:13).

a: a hidden door in the ceiling
p: The priests open a hidden hatch in the coffered ceiling and stone the king's party from above.
b: The phatnōma was a ceiling of sunken panels, as in Greek temples. From a hidden door in it the priests stone the men below, then cut them up and throw the heads out to the crowd. Death by a stone thrown from above is an old picture of shameful defeat: so Abimelech died, when "a woman threw an upper millstone down on Abimelech's head" (Judges 9:53).
orig: τὴν τοῦ φατνώματος κρυπτὴν θύραν (tēn tou phatnōmatos kryptēn thyran)

a: who handed over the ones who acted ungodly
t: Blessed be God, who handed them over
p: The blessing follows the old pattern of thanks after victory, as when Melchizedek blessed God for Abram's win.
b: Melchizedek blessed "God Most High, who has handed your enemies over to you" (Genesis 14:20). The letter blesses God in the same way for the death of a king. The verb "acted ungodly" (asebēsantas) is the book's judgment on the king who defiled the temple.
orig: ὃς ἔδωκεν τοὺς ἀσεβήσαντας (hos edōken tous asebēsantas)

a: the purification of the temple on the twenty-fifth of Kislev
p: 25 Kislev 164 BC: the day 1 Maccabees gives for the new altar's first sacrifice.
b: 1 Maccabees 4:52–54 dates the rededication to 25 Kislev in the year 148 (December 164 BC), three years to the day after the pagan altar's first sacrifice (1 Maccabees 1:59). 2 Maccabees 10:5 keeps the date, and 10:3 counts two years instead. Kislev is November–December; it is also the month in which Nehemiah's story begins (Nehemiah 1:1), a coincidence this letter may enjoy.

a: the feast of the fire
p: No other source knows a feast of Nehemiah's fire. The letter links Hanukkah's flame to the fire of the first temple.
b:
The letter wants Hanukkah to be more than a new festival. By tying it to Nehemiah's fire, which came from the altar of the first temple (1:19), it makes the rededication part of one unbroken worship from Solomon to Judas. 2 Maccabees 10:3 adds that Judas's priests struck stones to make new fire for the new altar.

Later names point the same way: Josephus says the feast was called "Lights" (Antiquities 12.325), and the Talmud tells of oil that burned for eight days (Shabbat 21b). None of these mentions a feast of fire, so the letter may be giving the lights a history.

a: when Nehemiah offered sacrifices after he had built the temple and the altar
p: Ezra says Jeshua and Zerubbabel built the altar and the temple. Nehemiah rebuilt the walls about seventy years later.
b:
Here the letter conflicts with the 66 books. In Ezra, "Jeshua son of Jozadak… and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel" built the altar (Ezra 3:2), and the house was finished under Darius in 515 BC (Ezra 6:15). Nehemiah came in 445 BC and rebuilt the city walls (Nehemiah 2–6). Sirach 49:11–13 keeps the same order: Zerubbabel and Jeshua built the house, Nehemiah the walls. No book of the 66 tells the story of the fire that follows.

Catholic readers often answer that the book is quoting a letter, and that reading Scripture well means weighing the kind of writing it is (Catechism 110). Others take the letter's Nehemiah as a symbol of the whole restoration after the exile.

a: when our ancestors were being led away to Persia
p: The exile was to Babylon, not Persia. The letter uses the later name for the lands of the east.
b: Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 586 BC, and the exiles were taken to Babylonia (2 Kings 25:11). Persia took over Babylon in 539 BC. By the second century BC "Persia" could stand for the whole east, and the letter uses it that way (1:12–13, 20, 33). The slip, if it is one, shows a writer more interested in the fire than in the map.

a: devout priests secretly took some of the fire from the altar
t: The fire that must not go out
p: The law said that the altar's fire must never go out. The story keeps the fire alive through the exile.
b: "Fire is to keep burning on the altar without a break. It is not to go out" (Leviticus 6:13). The first altar fire came from God himself (Leviticus 9:24), as Solomon's did (2 Chronicles 7:1). If the second temple's fire came from that same fire, its worship was the same worship. The Hebrew Bible says nothing of the kind, and the rabbis later counted the heavenly fire among five things the second temple lacked (Bavli Yoma 21b).

a: Nehemiah was sent by the king of Persia
p: Nehemiah 2:1–8 tells how Artaxerxes I sent his cupbearer to Jerusalem in 445 BC.
b: In the book of Nehemiah, the king grants Nehemiah leave, letters and timber to rebuild the walls (Nehemiah 2:5–8). The letter's Nehemiah is a temple founder and a priestly leader who orders priests about. The book of Nehemiah does show him reforming the temple's storerooms and the priests' duties (Nehemiah 13:4–13, 30–31).

a: only thick water
p: The "thick water" that catches fire in the sun is most likely naphtha, crude oil from seeps in Persia.
b: Oil wells and seeps were well known in the ancient east, and Greeks wondered at them. Plutarch tells how naphtha in Babylonia was shown to Alexander the Great, and how easily it caught fire (Life of Alexander 35). The story here may have grown up around such a substance. 1:36 seems to give its name.

a: a huge blaze was kindled
p: As on Mount Carmel, water poured on the offering comes before the fire.
b: Elijah had water poured three times over the wood and the sacrifice, and then "Down came the LORD's fire. It ate up the burnt offering, the wood, the stones and the dirt, and it licked up the water in the ditch" (1 Kings 18:38). In the letter the water itself becomes the fire, lit by the sun. Readers would hear both stories as proof that God accepts the sacrifice.

a: Jonathan began, and the others joined in, as Nehemiah did
p: The Greek hōs Neemiou is unclear: "as Nehemiah did," "with Nehemiah," or "as Nehemiah ordered."
b: The phrase hōs Neemiou ("as of Nehemiah") is short and hard. It may mean that Nehemiah joined the response, or that the rite followed his pattern. The KJV has "as Neemias did"; the Vulgate leaves it out and makes the prayer itself Nehemiah's (1:24, Nehemiæ erat oratio). Jonathan is not otherwise known as Nehemiah's priest. Nehemiah 12:11 names a Jonathan in the high priests' line.
orig: καταρχομένου Ἰωνάθου τῶν τε λοιπῶν ἐπιφωνούντων, ὡς Νεεμίου (katarchomenou Iōnathou tōn te loipōn epiphōnountōn, hōs Neemiou)

a: Lord God, maker of all things
p: The prayer stacks up titles of God, as the great prayers of the Persian period do.
b:
The prayer in Nehemiah 9:6, spoken by the Levites (the Septuagint gives it to Ezra), begins the same way, with God as maker of all things. The titles here, "the only King," "the only giver," "the only just one," stress that God alone is what Greek kings claimed to be: king, benefactor, judge. Paul's "the King of the ages… the only God" (1 Timothy 1:17) and "the only Ruler, the King of those who reign" (1 Timothy 6:15) sound the same note.

The prayer is a fair sample of Jewish worship in the Greek period, and parts of it have parallels in later synagogue prayers.

a: the kind one
p: The Greek chrēstos, "kind, good," is the word of the Greek Psalm "the Lord is good," quoted in 1 Peter 2:3.
b: In Greek, Psalm 34:8 reads "taste and see that the Lord is chrēstos"; the site's Plain from the Hebrew has "Taste and see: the LORD is good!" 1 Peter 2:3 quotes the Greek. The word belongs to everyday Greek for a kind, decent person, and it was also used in praise of kings.

a: the only giver
p: Chorēgos was the citizen who paid for a city's festival. God is the only real one.
b: In a Greek city the chorēgos paid for the choruses and festivals, and kings competed to be called benefactors. The prayer gives the title to God alone. The same verb returns in 3:3, where King Seleucus "paid" (chorēgein) the costs of the sacrifices: the book's first story will show which benefactor the temple can really rely on.

a: Keep your portion safe
p: Israel is God's "portion" or "share," as in the Song of Moses.
b: "For the LORD's own share is his people" (Deuteronomy 32:9). The Greek meris, "portion," makes the people of the Diaspora and of Judea alike God's own share among the nations. The prayer asks God to guard it and make it holy, two things the temple's purification was meant to show.

a: Bring our dispersed people together
p: The prayer asks God to gather the scattered Jews, the Diaspora. The letter is written to some of them.
b:
The word diaspora, "scattering," comes from the Greek Bible (Deuteronomy 28:25 LXX). The prophets promised that God would gather his scattered people (Deuteronomy 30:3–4; Isaiah 11:12; Psalm 147:2), and Nehemiah's prayer claims the promise (Nehemiah 1:9). The letter sends this prayer to Jews who had settled in Egypt: the hope of a gathering did not mean that they had to leave.

The New Testament takes up the hope: Jesus would die "to bring God's scattered children together into one" (John 11:52).
orig: ἐπισυνάγαγε τὴν διασπορὰν ἡμῶν (episynagage tēn diasporan hēmōn)
r: Deuteronomy 30:3–4; Isaiah 11:12; Psalm 147:2; Nehemiah 1:9; John 11:52; James 1:1

a: Let the nations know that you are our God
t: So that the nations may know
p: Solomon prayed that the temple would make God known "so that every people on earth will know that the LORD is God."
b: The prayer asks for the same result Solomon asked for: "so that every people on earth will know that the LORD is God" (1 Kings 8:60). In 2 Maccabees the nations do come to know it: Heliodorus (3:36–39) and even Antiochus (9:17) confess the power of Israel's God.

a: as Moses said
p: Moses' song promised that God would "bring them in and plant them" on his own mountain.
b: The Song of the Sea says, "You will bring them in and plant them" (Exodus 15:17), on the mountain and holy place God made. The prayer applies the promise to the people of the second temple period, many of whom lived far from it.

a: sang the hymns to the harp
p: The verb epipsallō means to sing with a stringed instrument.
b: The priests answer the prayer with music, as the Levites did at Solomon's dedication, when the singers praised God together with the instruments (2 Chronicles 5:12–13). Greek psallō, "pluck strings," is the root of "psalm."

a: swallowed up by the light that shone back from the altar
p: A second flame flares up from the stones, but the altar's fire swallows it.
b: The detail is hard to picture, and its point may be that there is only one sacred fire. Whatever burns away from the altar is taken back into the altar's light. Some readers connect it with the stones on which Judas later struck the new fire (10:3), since both stories end in a single fire on the altar.

a: made it sacred
p: The story has the Persian king test the wonder and make the place a sacred site.
b: The Persians held fire in honor, so a fire that came from water would impress a Persian king. The letter has him test the matter (dokimasas), fence it in and draw revenue from it. Like Cyrus, Darius and Artaxerxes in Ezra and Nehemiah, he is a foreign ruler who honors Israel's God. In 3:2–3 Seleucus will do the same.

a: gave it the name Nephthar
p: The name looks like "naphtha," crude oil. Its meaning "purification" is the letter's own explanation.
b: No Hebrew or Persian word "nephthar" meaning "purification" is known. The name is most likely naphtha, the Greek word (from the east) for petroleum. The letter explains it as "purification" because Nehemiah "purified the sacrifices" with it (1:33). Swete's Greek has Nephthar both times, which makes the last sentence strange; Venetus has Nephthai the second time, and the Vulgate and KJV have "Nephi." See the variant.

a: It is found in the records
p: The source is not the book of Jeremiah. Other Jewish writings, and the Orthodox lives of the saints, also tell of Jeremiah hiding the ark.
b:
The "records" (apographai) are not named, and no book of the 66 contains the story. Similar stories survive elsewhere. The Lives of the Prophets, a Jewish work of about the first century AD, says Jeremiah hid the ark in a rock and that it will be the first thing raised at the resurrection. In 2 Baruch 6:7–10 an angel hides the temple's holy things before the Babylonians come.

The Orthodox synaxarion for 1 May, the day of the prophet Jeremiah, retells the same tradition. The Talmud has another: King Josiah hid the ark (Bavli Yoma 52b, from 2 Chronicles 35:3).

a: Jeremiah the prophet
p: In Codex Alexandrinus, the words from "prophet" in 2:1 to "go along" in 2:4 were written in the margins and over an erasure by a later hand.
b: Swete's note reads: φητης οτι εκελευσεν…αυτω συν ακολουθειν in mgg et sup ras Aᵃ. A corrector (Aᵃ) scraped off what the first scribe wrote and wrote this passage over the erasure and into the margins. What the first hand had is unknown, probably the same text with a copying slip. The Plain follows Swete's text, which is the corrected one.
orig: φητης οτι εκελευσεν...αυτω συν ακολουθειν in mgg et sup ras Aᵃ

a: Jeremiah the prophet told the people being carried off
p: In the book of Jeremiah, the prophet stays in Judah after 586 BC and is later taken to Egypt. He does not go with the exiles or to Nebo.
b:
The letter has Jeremiah instruct "the people being carried off," then lead the tent and the ark to Moses' mountain in Moab (2:1–5). The book of Jeremiah tells another story. The Babylonians freed him from the guard court and let him stay in the land (Jeremiah 39:11–14; 40:1–6), and after Gedaliah's murder he was taken to Egypt against his will (Jeremiah 43:6–7). It never puts him among the deportees or at Nebo. Here the letter goes beyond the 66 books, and may conflict with them.

The letter gives no date for the hiding. An earlier deportation, in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:10–16), is one possible setting, but the book of Jeremiah says nothing of it either. Jeremiah 27:19–22 expects the temple's vessels to go to Babylon and come back, not to be hidden.

a: images of gold and silver and the finery on them
p: Jeremiah warns the exiles against the idols they will see, as in the Letter of Jeremiah.
b: Jeremiah wrote from Jerusalem to the exiles in Babylon (Jeremiah 29:1–23), and Jeremiah 10:3–9 mocks idols covered with silver and gold. The deuterocanonical Letter of Jeremiah expands that warning: the exiles will see gods of silver, gold and wood carried on shoulders, decked in clothes, and must not fear them. 2 Maccabees seems to know such a tradition. Its own readers in Egypt lived among temples full of images.
r: Jeremiah 10:3–9; Jeremiah 29:1–23; Letter of Jeremiah 4–11; Isaiah 44:9–20

a: the tent and the ark
p: The "tent" is the tabernacle of Moses, which Solomon brought into the temple with the ark.
b: Solomon's priests "carried up the LORD's ark, with the tent of meeting and all the holy objects that were in the tent" (1 Kings 8:4). Nothing in Kings or Chronicles says what became of the ark when Babylon burned the temple in 586 BC. 2 Kings 25:13–17 lists the bronze objects taken, but not the ark. Chronicles says only that the ark's poles were still in place "until today" (2 Chronicles 5:9). This gap made room for the stories of its hiding.
orig: τὴν σκηνὴν καὶ τὴν κιβωτὸν (tēn skēnēn kai tēn kibōton)

a: the mountain that Moses had climbed when he saw God's inheritance
p: The mountain is Nebo in Moab, from which Moses saw the promised land before he died.
b: "Moses climbed from the plains of Moab up Mount Nebo, to the peak of Pisgah… There the LORD let him see the whole land" (Deuteronomy 34:1). The ark is hidden where the first leader of Israel looked into the land he could not enter. The story suggests that it waits, like the people, for a future entry.

a: the altar of incense
p: The gold altar stood before the curtain, "in front of the atonement lid." Hebrews 9:4 places it with the ark.
b: The altar of incense was to stand "in front of the veil that hangs before the ark of the testimony" (Exodus 30:6). Hebrews 9:4 describes the inner room as "having a golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant," close to this list. The Greek thymiatērion in Hebrews can also mean a censer.

a: The place will stay unknown
p: The story goes beyond the 66 books. Jeremiah 3:16 says the ark will not be missed. Revelation 11:19 sees it in heaven.
b:
Jeremiah's own book says that in the days to come people will not say any more, "The ark of the LORD's covenant!" It will not rise in their hearts, and no one will make another (Jeremiah 3:16). The ark's loss there is final, and God's presence no longer needs it. 2 Maccabees instead keeps the ark hidden until the end. John's vision answers in its own way: "the ark of his covenant could be seen in his temple" in heaven (Revelation 11:19).

Jewish tradition is divided: some rabbis say the ark went to Babylon, others that it was hidden under the temple (Mishnah Shekalim 6:1–2; Bavli Yoma 53b–54a). Revelation's promise of "the hidden manna" (Revelation 2:17) belongs to the same hope, since a jar of manna was kept before the ark (Exodus 16:33–34). Whether Mary is the new ark is asked on the card at 2 Samuel 6.

a: The glory of the Lord will be seen, and the cloud
p: The cloud and the glory filled Moses' tabernacle and Solomon's temple. Jeremiah promises they will be seen again.
b: At the end of Exodus, "The cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the LORD's glory filled the tabernacle" (Exodus 40:34). At Solomon's dedication "the cloud filled the LORD's house" (1 Kings 8:10). The second temple had no such sign, and Ezekiel had seen the glory leave (Ezekiel 10:18–19) and return in a vision (Ezekiel 43:2–5). The Gospels put the cloud on the mountain of the transfiguration (Matthew 17:5).
r: Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11; 2 Chronicles 5:13–14; Ezekiel 43:2–5; Matthew 17:5; Revelation 15:8

a: a sacrifice of dedication
p: The Greek enkainismos, "dedication," gives the feast its Greek name. John 10:22 calls it ta enkainia.
b: The same word family is used for Solomon's dedication of the temple in the Greek of 1 Kings 8:63 ("dedicated the LORD's house"), for the altar Judas dedicated (1 Maccabees 4:56, 59), and for the feast in John 10:22. By linking Solomon's dedication with Judas's, the letter gives Hanukkah a biblical model. Hebrew hanukkah means the same thing.

a: fire came down from heaven
p: Leviticus 9:24 and 2 Chronicles 7:1 tell of fire from God. Leviticus does not say Moses prayed for it.
b: Of Solomon, 2 Chronicles says: "Solomon had just finished praying when fire came down out of the heavens" (2 Chronicles 7:1). Of Moses' day, Leviticus says only that "Fire came out from before the LORD and ate up the burnt offering" (Leviticus 9:24), at the first sacrifice of Aaron. The letter makes both answers to prayer. It agrees with the 66 books on the fire, and goes beyond them on Moses' prayer.

a: Because the sin offering had not been eaten, it was burned up
t: A saying of Moses not found in the law
p: No such words of Moses appear in the law. Leviticus 10:16–20 is the nearest passage, and there Moses is angry that the offering was burned.
b: In Leviticus 10:16–20, Moses finds that the goat of the sin offering "had been burned" and asks Aaron's sons, "Why did you not eat the sin offering in the holy place?" Aaron answers, and Moses accepts it. 2 Maccabees gives Moses a different saying, which explains a miracle: because no one ate the offering, God's fire burned it all. Commentators find no exact source and think the letter draws on a tradition or a free reading of Leviticus. It goes beyond the 66 books here.

a: Solomon kept the eight days
p: Solomon's dedication ended on an eighth day. The letter offers it as a model for Hanukkah's eight days.
b: Chronicles says, "On the eighth day they held a closing gathering. They had kept the altar's dedication for seven days and the feast for seven days" (2 Chronicles 7:9). The dedication was joined to the Feast of Booths, which also ends with an eighth day (Leviticus 23:36). The letter has two models for the eight days of Hanukkah, then: Solomon and Booths (1:9, 18).

a: in the memoirs from Nehemiah's time
p: The book of Nehemiah contains a first-person memoir, but it says nothing about a library or a fire.
b: Much of the book of Nehemiah is told by Nehemiah himself ("The record of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah," Nehemiah 1:1), and scholars call it his memoir. The letter claims a wider "Nehemiah literature," with records and memoirs. These may be lost writings, or a way of giving its traditions an old source.
orig: ἐν τοῖς ὑπομνηματισμοῖς τοῖς κατὰ τὸν Νεεμίαν (en tois hypomnēmatismois tois kata ton Neemian)

a: he laid the foundation of a library
p: Many scholars read the verse as a glimpse of the Hebrew Bible taking shape: the Prophets, the Psalms and the royal records.
b:
The "books about the kings and prophets" may be the books Jews call the Prophets (Joshua to Kings, and Isaiah to Malachi), and "David's books" the Psalms. The "letters from kings about gifts" fit the Persian decrees of Ezra 6–7. The Jewish canon was later counted as the Law, the Prophets and the Writings, and the prologue to Sirach, written in Egypt soon after 132 BC, speaks of the law, the prophets and the rest that came after them.

Roger Beckwith uses this verse in arguing that the Hebrew canon was settled long before the Christian era; others think it shows only that books were being collected, and note that it says nothing of which books counted. Whether 2 Maccabees itself is Scripture is asked on the card on the book page.

a: letters from kings about gifts to the temple
p: Persian kings sent letters granting gifts and funds to the temple, which Ezra quotes.
b: Ezra quotes Cyrus's memo (Ezra 6:3–5), Darius's order to pay the costs "out of the king's funds" (Ezra 6:8), and Artaxerxes' letter sending "the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have offered of their own free will" (Ezra 7:15). The Greek anathemata are gifts dedicated to a temple. Chapter 3 begins with such royal gifts (3:2–3).
orig: ἐπιστολὰς βασιλέων περὶ ἀναθεμάτων (epistolas basileōn peri anathematōn)

a: Judas did the same
p: Antiochus's officers had burned the books of the law (1 Maccabees 1:56). The letter has Judas gather what was left.
b: 1 Maccabees 1:56–57 says the king's men tore up and burned the scrolls of the law, and that anyone found with one was put to death. The letter answers with Judas the collector, a second Nehemiah. Nothing else is known of this collection. The claim fits the letter's purpose: Jerusalem, not Egypt, holds the books and can share them.

a: send messengers to carry them back to you
p: The offer of books ties the Jews of Egypt to Jerusalem. Other sources tell of scrolls brought from Jerusalem to Egypt.
b: The Letter of Aristeas tells how the high priest sent scrolls of the law from Jerusalem to Alexandria, with seventy-two translators. Ben Sira's grandson came to Egypt in 132 BC and translated his grandfather's book there, as his prologue says. The letter's offer fits that pattern: the homeland supplies the texts and the feast, and Egypt receives them. Some scholars also read it as a quiet rebuke of the rival temple at Leontopolis (see the chapter page).

a: with the kingdom, the priesthood and the holiness
t: A kingdom, a priesthood, a holy nation
p: The list echoes God's promise at Sinai: "a kingdom of priests, a holy nation." 1 Peter 2:9 uses the same Greek.
b: At Sinai God said, "you will be for me a kingdom of priests, a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6). The Greek of that verse, basileion hierateuma, is the very pair this verse uses, and 1 Peter 2:9 calls Christians "a royal priesthood, a holy nation" with the same words. Revelation says Christ "made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father" (Revelation 1:6). The letter claims the promise for Judea after the victory; the New Testament gives it to the church.
orig: τὸ βασίλειον καὶ τὸ ἱεράτευμα καὶ τὸν ἁγιασμόν (to basileion kai to hierateuma kai ton hagiasmon)

a: bring us together from all that lies under heaven to the holy place
p: The letter ends with the hope of the Diaspora's return, promised in Deuteronomy 30.
b: "Even if you have been driven to the farthest edge of the sky, the LORD your God will gather you from there" (Deuteronomy 30:4). The purified temple is the sign that the promise has begun to be kept. Jesus speaks of angels who "will gather together his chosen from the four winds" (Matthew 24:31).

a: Judas Maccabeus
p: The writer's preface starts here, with the hero's name. 2 Maccabees never names his father Mattathias.
b: On the name "Maccabeus," probably "the hammer," see 1 Maccabees 2:4. Unlike 1 Maccabees, this book tells nothing of Mattathias and his revolt: Judas appears suddenly at 5:27 and 8:1. The book is the story of a temple and of God's help, more than of a family.

a: Antiochus Epiphanes and his son Eupator
p: Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175–164 BC) and his young son Antiochus V Eupator (164–162 BC).
b: "Epiphanes" means "God made manifest," a title Antiochus IV used on his coins. Critics punned it into Epimanes, "the madman" (Polybius 26.1). His son, a boy when he became king, was called Eupator, "of a good father." The book also covers the start of Demetrius I's reign and ends with Nicanor's defeat in 161 BC (15:36).

a: the appearances from heaven
p: Epiphaneia, an "appearance" or "manifestation" of God, is one of the book's key words, and it mocks the king's title Epiphanes.
b:
The book promises the reader stories of God's epiphaneiai, "appearances," and gives them: the horseman and the young men (3:24–26), riders in the sky (5:2–4), horsemen in battle (10:29–30; 11:8), and "the appearance of the one who sees all things" (12:22; and at 15:27 in Venetus). The king who called himself Epiphanes, "God manifest," meets the God who really appears.

The New Testament uses the word for Christ's coming: "the appearance of the glory of our great God and Savior" (Titus 2:13; 2 Timothy 1:10).
orig: τὰς ἐξ οὐρανοῦ γενομένας ἐπιφανείας (tas ex ouranou genomenas epiphaneias)

a: for Judaism
p: This is the oldest known use of the word Ioudaismos, "Judaism": the Jewish way of life, set against "the Greek way."
b: The Greek Ioudaismos appears first here and again in 8:1 and 14:38. The book coins or uses it as the opposite of Hellēnismos, "the Greek way" (4:13). It means loyalty to the law and the ancestral customs, not yet a "religion" in the modern sense. Paul uses the word of his own past: "I was going further in Judaism than many my own age" (Galatians 1:13–14).

a: the barbarian crowds
p: Greeks called foreigners barbarians. This Jewish writer, writing in fine Greek, turns the word on the Greek armies.
b: For Greeks, barbaroi were people who did not speak Greek. The writer of 2 Maccabees writes polished Greek and calls the Seleucid army "barbarian," and uses the word again of Israel's enemies (10:4; compare 4:25; 5:22). The reversal is deliberate: the true civilization is the Jewish way of life.

a: Jason of Cyrene told all this in five books
p: The writer says he is shortening a five-volume history by Jason of Cyrene. Nothing else is known of Jason or his work.
b:
Cyrene, on the coast of modern Libya, had a large Jewish community: a Simon of Cyrene carried Jesus' cross (Mark 15:21), and men of Cyrene were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10). Jason's five books are lost, and no ancient writer quotes them. Most scholars accept that he existed and wrote soon after the events, since his history ends in 161 BC.

The book we have is the "epitome," the shortened version; Clement of Alexandria calls its writer "the composer of the epitome." How much is Jason and how much the epitomist is debated.
orig: ὑπὸ Ἰάσωνος τοῦ Κυρηναίου δεδηλωμένα διὰ πέντε βιβλίων (hypo Iasōnos tou Kyrēnaiou dedēlōmena dia pente bibliōn)

a: the flood of numbers
p: The Greek may mean the mass of figures in Jason's work (dates, troops, the dead), or just its great length.
b: To chyma tōn arithmōn is "the outpouring of numbers." Readers of Hellenistic history knew pages full of army sizes and casualty counts, and Jason may have had many. Others take "numbers" as the number of lines or books. Either way the writer promises a shorter, easier read.
orig: τὸ χύμα τῶν ἀριθμῶν (to chyma tōn arithmōn)

a: to give enjoyment to those who want to read
p: Greek and Roman writers said a good book should please and profit. The writer claims both.
b: Historians of the time debated whether history should entertain or only instruct. The Roman poet Horace put the common view in a line: the one who mixes the useful with the sweet wins every vote (Ars Poetica 343). The writer aims at psychagōgia, "delight," and ōpheleia, "benefit." Paul uses a related word when he says all Scripture is "useful" (ōphelimos, 2 Timothy 3:16).

a: It is a matter of sweat and sleepless nights
p: The writer describes his labor, unlike a prophet. Churches weigh this differently when they ask whether the book is inspired.
b:
The prophets say "Thus says the LORD." This writer tells us how hard he worked to summarize another man's book. Luke also describes careful research (Luke 1:1–4), so a human author's labor is not unique to 2 Maccabees.

Catholic teaching holds that God chose human authors who wrote "as true authors," using their own powers (Dei Verbum 11; Catechism 106), so the writer's toil does not count against inspiration. William Whitaker (1588) and other Protestant writers have read his modesty, here and in "thin and middling" at 15:38, as the mark of a book written without inspiration. Whether that admission rules out inspiration is asked on the second card on the book page.

a: someone who prepares a banquet
p: The writer pictures himself as a host who works to please his guests. He ends the book with a picture from the table too (15:39).
b: The host at a symposion, a Greek dinner party, thinks of his guests' pleasure, not his own. The image frames the whole book: at its end the writer compares good style to wine mixed with water, which is pleasant to drink (15:39). Readers are guests, and the history is served to suit them.

a: we wear ourselves out
p: The Greek atoneō usually means "to grow slack, faint." Here it seems to mean straining until worn out.
b: The participle atonountes should mean "flagging, being worn out," which seems odd beside "following the outlines." The KJV has "labouring to follow." The Plain keeps the sense of tiring effort, in line with the "sweat and sleepless nights" of 2:26.

a: the one who first wrote the history
p: The writer calls Jason the archēgenetēs, the "founder" or "original author" of the history.
b: The writer separates two jobs. The historian goes into every detail, "walks around" the subject and gets things exact. The abridger, like the painter of a finished house (2:29), makes it pleasant and short. He is honest that he did not research the events himself. Readers in every age have asked how this affects the book's reliability; see the book page.

a: the one who retells it
p: Metaphrasis means a retelling in other words, not a translation. The writer claims a hand in the style.
b: The Greek metaphrasis is used of putting a text into new words, a paraphrase. Combined with the image of the painter (2:29), it shows that the writer did more than cut: he shaped the language and the drama. The book's rhetoric, speeches and comments on God's purposes (for example 4:16–17; 5:17–20; 6:12–17) are usually credited to him.
orig: τῷ τὴν μετάφρασιν ποιουμένῳ (tō tēn metaphrasin poioumenō)

a: People lived in the holy city in complete peace
p: The story starts in a time of peace under a godly high priest, so that the fall that follows stands out.
b: Chapter 3 pictures Jerusalem as it should be: the law kept, the high priest godly, even pagan kings paying for the sacrifices. The pattern of the book follows: when the people are faithful, God guards the temple (3); when they sin, he lets it be defiled (4–5; 5:17–20); when they repent and martyrs die, he returns (7:37–38; 8:5). 1 Maccabees starts instead with Alexander and the Greek kings, and has no such golden age.

a: Onias the high priest
p: Onias III, high priest about 190s to 175 BC, son of the Simon whom Sirach praises. He was murdered about 170 BC (4:33–35).
b:
Onias III belonged to the old high-priestly family descended from Zadok. His father Simon II is praised in Sirach 50:1–21 as the greatest of his brothers and the strength of his people, who repaired the temple. Onias was pushed out by his brother Jason (4:7) and later killed near Antioch (4:33–35). In 15:12 he appears in Judas's dream, praying for the people.

Many scholars find him in Daniel's visions: the "anointed one" who is "cut off" (Daniel 9:26) and the "prince of the covenant" who is broken (Daniel 11:22).

a: even the kings honored the place
p: Antiochus III, about 200 BC, gave silver, wheat, wine, oil and salt for the sacrifices, as Josephus records.
b: When Antiochus III took Judea from the Ptolemies, he wrote that he would supply the sacrifices with "twenty thousand pieces of silver" and set amounts of flour, wheat and salt, and freed the council of elders, the priests, the temple scribes and the singers from taxes (Josephus, Antiquities 12.138–144). Persian kings had done the same (Ezra 6:8–10; 7:15–23). So the claim of 3:2–3 has support.

a: Seleucus, king of Asia
p: Seleucus IV Philopator (187–175 BC), son of Antiochus III and older brother of Antiochus IV.
b: "King of Asia" was a Seleucid title (1 Maccabees 8:6; 11:13). Seleucus IV inherited a kingdom burdened by the huge payments that Rome had imposed on his father at Apamea in 188 BC. A king who needed money is the background of the whole chapter. Daniel 11:20 is often read of him: one who will "send a tax-gatherer through the splendor of the kingdom" and soon be broken.

a: the appointed overseer of the temple
p: The Greek prostatēs was an administrator, probably in charge of the temple's business. Simon was the brother of Menelaus (4:23).
b: The office is not clear. A prostatēs in a Greek temple managed its property and dealings with outsiders. Simon's quarrel is about the city's market (agoranomia), the office that controlled weights, prices and trade, an important source of money and power. Simon's brother Menelaus later buys the high priesthood (4:23–25).

a: from the tribe of Benjamin
p: A Benjaminite could not be a priest. Some Latin and Armenian copies read "Bilgah," a priestly family whose disgrace the rabbis remembered.
b:
Bilgah was one of the twenty-four priestly divisions: "the fifteenth for Bilgah" (1 Chronicles 24:14; compare Nehemiah 12:5). If Simon came from it, his family's later shame would make sense. The Mishnah says the division of Bilgah was punished, with its ring for the sacrifices fixed and its niche shut (Mishnah Sukkah 5:8). The Talmud explains that Miriam of the house of Bilgah left her faith, married a soldier of the Greek kings and struck the altar (Bavli Sukkah 56b).

The Greek has "Benjamin," and an overseer need not have been a priest. Bullard and Hatton, who report the Bilgah reading, themselves take "Benjamin" as the name of a priestly family, Miniamin (Nehemiah 12:17, 41), and prefer "of the Benjamin family." See the variant.

a: Apollonius son of Thrasaeus
p: The father's name is spelled several ways in the manuscripts and versions.
b: Swete prints Thrasaeus (Thrasaiou) from Alexandrinus. Venetus has Tharsiou or Tharseou, Hort conjectured Tharsea, and the Vulgate has Tharsææ filium. Many Apolloniuses served the Seleucids (4:4, 21; 5:24; 1 Maccabees 3:10), so the father's name was meant to tell them apart.

a: governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia
p: The Seleucid province that included Judea, taken from the Ptolemies in 200 BC.
b: "Coele-Syria," "Hollow Syria," first meant the Beqaa valley between the Lebanon ranges, then the whole land south of it to Egypt. Antiochus III won it from Ptolemy V at the battle of Panium in 200 BC. An inscription found in Israel, the Heliodorus stele, shows Seleucus IV writing to Heliodorus in 178 BC to appoint a man named Olympiodoros over the temples of "Coele-Syria and Phoenicia," the same phrase as here.

a: the treasury at Jerusalem
p: Ancient temples kept the savings of the rich and the poor. Jerusalem's did too, as Josephus says.
b: Temples were the safest places in a city, and people left money there in trust. Nehemiah describes storerooms in the temple for gifts and tithes (Nehemiah 13:4–5). Josephus says that when the Romans burned the temple in AD 70 they burned the treasury chambers, where "the entire riches of the Jews were heaped up together" (Jewish War 6.282). Simon's claim is that the money did not belong to the sacrifices and so could be taken.

a: Heliodorus, his chief minister
p: Heliodorus is known from inscriptions. He later had Seleucus IV murdered, Appian says.
b:
The title "over the affairs" (ho epi tōn pragmatōn) means the king's chief minister. A stone found in Israel and published in 2007 preserves Seleucus IV's letter to Heliodorus of 178 BC, appointing an overseer for the temples of the province, part of the same drive for revenue. Its lower part was found at Maresha in the excavations of 2005–2006.

In 175 BC Heliodorus plotted against Seleucus, and Appian says he had him killed (Syrian Wars 45). Daniel 11:20 is often read of Seleucus and his "tax-gatherer."
orig: Ἡλιόδωρον τὸν ἐπὶ τῶν πραγμάτων (Hēliodōron ton epi tōn pragmatōn)

a: deposits belonging to widows and orphans
p: The law's care for widows and orphans is at stake. To rob the temple would be to rob them.
b: God's law commands: "Never treat a widow or a fatherless child harshly" (Exodus 22:22), and makes them guests at Israel's feasts (Deuteronomy 14:29). Onias answers the king's claim with the law. The New Testament keeps the concern: "pure religion" is to look after orphans and widows (James 1:27), and Jesus condemns those who "eat up widows' houses" (Mark 12:40).

a: Hyrcanus son of Tobias
p: Hyrcanus belonged to the rich Tobiad family east of the Jordan. Josephus tells his story.
b:
Josephus tells of Joseph son of Tobias, a tax farmer for the Ptolemies, and his youngest son Hyrcanus. Hyrcanus settled "beyond Jordan," built a fortress of white stone with carved animals and caves cut in the rock, called the place "Tyre," and ruled there seven years under Seleucus. He killed himself when Antiochus IV came to the throne (Antiquities 12.228–236). The remains at 'Iraq al-Amir in Jordan are usually identified with his fortress.

The family may go back to "Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite" of Nehemiah 2:10. Hyrcanus favored the Ptolemies, which may have made his deposits a target.

a: its right of sanctuary
p: The Greek asylia meant a temple's legal right not to be robbed or entered by force.
b: Hellenistic cities and temples asked kings to recognize their asylia, "inviolability": no one could seize property or people within them. Onias argues in the language of Greek law as well as the law of Moses. A temple "honored all over the world" (see 2:22; 5:16) should be safe from the king's own officer.

a: the one who gave the law about money left in trust
p: The priests appeal to the law of Exodus 22 about goods left with a neighbor.
b: "If someone gives his neighbor money or things to keep for him, and they are stolen from the man's house, then if the thief is found, he repays two for one" (Exodus 22:7). Leviticus 6:2–5 treats lying about a deposit as a sin against God. The priests ask the lawgiver to keep his own law: the God who commanded that deposits be kept safe should keep these.

a: Women wrapped sackcloth below their breasts
p: The whole city takes part in the plea, even the young women usually kept at home. 3 Maccabees tells a very similar scene.
b:
Sackcloth was the dress of mourning and pleading (Esther 4:1–3; Jonah 3:5–8; Joel 1:13). Unmarried girls of good families were kept indoors, a custom Philo also describes (Special Laws 3.169). That they run to the gates and walls shows the danger.

3 Maccabees 1:8–2:24 tells how Ptolemy IV tried to enter the holy of holies: young women "shut up in their chambers" rush out (3 Maccabees 1:18–19), the high priest prays, and God strikes the king down. 4 Maccabees 4:1–14 retells this chapter with Apollonius in Heliodorus's place.

a: stretched out their hands toward heaven
p: The posture of prayer in Israel: Solomon "lifted his open palms to the heavens."
b: At the temple's dedication Solomon "lifted his open palms to the heavens" (1 Kings 8:22), and the psalmist prays "when I raise my hands toward the inner room of your holy place" (Psalm 28:2). Paul asks that people pray "lifting up holy hands" (1 Timothy 2:8).

a: the Sovereign of spirits and of all authority
p: God is called dynastēs, "Sovereign," over the spirits and every power.
b: The title recalls Moses' "God of the spirits of all flesh" (Numbers 16:22) and 1 Enoch's favorite name for God, "the Lord of Spirits" (1 Enoch 37–71). The "spirits" are the angels who are about to act. Paul uses the same word for God, the blessed and only dynastēs (1 Timothy 6:15). The KJV has "the Lord of spirits, and the Prince of all power"; on the Latin, see the variant.
orig: ὁ τῶν πνευμάτων καὶ πάσης ἐξουσίας δυνάστης (ho tōn pneumatōn kai pasēs exousias dynastēs)

a: a horse with a fearsome rider
p: Horses and riders from heaven appear in Kings, Zechariah and Revelation, and again later in this book.
b: Elisha's servant saw "the hill was filled with horses and fiery chariots, surrounding Elisha" (2 Kings 6:17). Zechariah saw a man on a red horse (Zechariah 1:8), and John saw "a white horse! The one riding it is called Faithful and True" (Revelation 19:11). In 2 Maccabees riders appear in the sky over Jerusalem (5:2–3) and fight beside Judas (10:29–30; 11:8). The golden armor marks the rider as heavenly. Raphael painted this scene in the Vatican (1511–1512).
l: The Expulsion of Heliodorus from the Temple
The Expulsion of Heliodorus from the Temple

a: Two other young men
p: The young men are angels. In the Gospels, too, angels at the tomb appear as young men or men in white.
b:
In Tobit the angel Raphael appears as a young man (Tobit 5:5). At Jesus' tomb Mark has "a young man" in white (Mark 16:5), Luke two men in shining clothes (Luke 24:4), and John "two angels dressed in white" (John 20:12). Angels who strike the proud appear in 2 Kings 19:35 and Acts 12:23.

Some scholars, following Bickerman, think two versions of the story have been joined: one in which the horse tramples Heliodorus, and one in which the young men flog him and later grant him life (3:33).
r: Tobit 5:5; Mark 16:5; Luke 24:4; John 20:12; Acts 12:23; 2 Kings 19:35

a: he had plainly come to know the sovereign power
p: In Swete's Greek, Heliodorus recognizes the power. In the KJV, the men who carry him do.
b: The participle epegnōkota is accusative, agreeing with "him": Heliodorus himself has come to know the sovereignty. Venetus adds "of God." Rahlfs prints a nominative plural, epegnōkotes, which makes the bearers the subject, and the KJV agrees: "manifestly they acknowledged the power of God." The Plain follows the Greek. The difference shapes the story: it is the enemy who learns. See the variant.
orig: φανερῶς τὴν δυναστίαν ἐπεγνωκότα (phanerōs tēn dynasteian epegnōkota)

a: who had shown his own place to be marvelous
t: God guards his place, but not always
p: Here God defends the temple. In 5:17–20 he lets Antiochus rob it. The book explains the difference.
b:
In chapter 3 the temple is untouchable. Two chapters later Antiochus IV takes 1,800 talents from it unharmed (5:21), and the writer explains: the people had sinned, and "the Lord did not choose the nation for the sake of the place; he chose the place for the sake of the nation" (5:19). The place shares the people's fortunes.

The prophets had already warned against trusting the temple as a charm (Jeremiah 7:4). Jesus speaks of "something greater than the temple" (Matthew 12:6). Whether any place is holy in this way is asked on the card on the chapter page.
orig: τὸν κύριον εὐλόγουν τὸν παραδοξάζοντα τὸν ἑαυτοῦ τόπον (ton paradoxazonta ton heautou topon)

a: now that the Almighty Lord had appeared
p: Where the sense needs "Lord," Codex Alexandrinus writes the short form for "Christ," a one-letter slip.
b: Christian scribes wrote sacred names in short forms with a line above: ΚΥ for kyriou, "of the Lord," and ΧΥ for Christou, "of Christ." Swete's note says A has ΧΥ here (κυριου] χυ A), which would give "the Almighty Christ appeared." Swete, like every editor, prints "Lord." The slip shows Christian hands copying the book, and perhaps a Christian reading of its "appearances."

a: making the atonement
p: Hilasmos, "atonement," is the word 1 John uses of Christ. Here the high priest makes it for a pagan officer.
b: The Greek hilasmos renders the language of atonement (Hebrew kipper, "make atonement"). 1 John 2:2 uses the same word of Christ, whose atonement reaches the sins of the whole world, not only those of believers. Onias's sacrifice is offered for an enemy, and it works: the angels tell Heliodorus he owes his life to it.

a: he brought a sacrifice for the man's rescue
p: The temple offered sacrifices for foreign rulers. Stopping them in AD 66 was an act of war.
b: Darius funded offerings so that the priests might "pray for the life of the king and of his sons" (Ezra 6:10), and Jews in Roman times sacrificed daily for the emperor. Josephus says that in AD 66 the temple captain Eleazar persuaded the priests to accept no gift or sacrifice from a foreigner, and that this was the beginning of the war with Rome (Jewish War 2.409). Onias's sacrifice for a pagan officer reflects the older, open custom, and also a politician's caution.

a: Be very grateful to Onias the high priest
p: Heliodorus lives because of the high priest's prayer, as Abimelech lived by Abraham's and Job's friends by Job's.
b: God tells Abimelech, "He is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you will live" (Genesis 20:7), and tells Job's friends, "Job my servant will pray for you. I will accept him" (Job 42:8). James says that a righteous person's prayer, when it is at work, is very strong (James 5:16). Here the righteous man is the high priest, and the one prayed for is the enemy of the temple. Whether the saints in heaven pray for people on earth is a different question, asked on the card at Revelation 5.

a: made very great vows
p: Like Naaman, the foreign officer goes home to worship the God of Israel. Daniel's kings do the same.
b: Naaman said, "Look, I know it now: there is no God in all the earth, only in Israel" (2 Kings 5:15). Heliodorus offers sacrifice, makes vows and becomes a witness to "the works of the greatest God" (3:36). Nebuchadnezzar and Darius do the same in Daniel (Daniel 4:34–37; 6:25–27). The book uses the pattern again for Antiochus IV (9:12–17).

a: send him there
p: The advice is bitter humor: send your enemies to Jerusalem. Heliodorus himself later killed the king.
b: The king asks whom to send next, and Heliodorus answers with a joke at the expense of anyone who would plot against the king. The irony was not lost on readers who knew that Heliodorus himself plotted against Seleucus and, Appian says, had him killed (Syrian Wars 45). The book's next chapter shows Simon still slandering Onias (4:1–2).

a: He who has his home in heaven is himself the overseer and helper of that place
t: The God in heaven guards the place on earth
p: The God who lives in heaven watches over the temple on earth, as Solomon prayed.
b: Solomon asked God to "listen from the place where you live, from the heavens" to every prayer made toward the temple (1 Kings 8:30). The psalms join the two: God's seat is in the heavens (Psalm 123:1), yet he guards Zion (Psalm 121:4; Psalm 48). Heliodorus's confession puts the point in a pagan's mouth. The card on the chapter page asks whether any place now has such protection.

a: That is how things turned out
p: The writer closes his stories with such summary lines. They mark the parts of the book.
b: The formula "and the things about Heliodorus… turned out this way" closes a section, as similar lines do later in the book (7:42; 10:9; 13:26; 15:37). The first story of the book, the temple saved, is complete. The second, the temple's fall through the high priests' rivalry, begins in 4:1.
